title: Building with AI isn't hard. It is the harness that stops me shipping mistakes.
author: DarrenMoore
selftext:
I built a browser strategy game solo 100% with AI. It was and still is an AI experiment but it's also turned into an evening hobby project. Three months live, real players. It writes a confident, well-structured change that quietly breaks and I've been an idiot to trust it multiple times.

The hot topic right now is "AI Loops" and your harness and tests are a **critical** prerequisite for that to work.

So a lot of my time wasn't getting it to write code. It was building the layer of gates around it that every change passes before it reaches live. That layer grew one incident at a time. Something broke in production, I asked the AI to fix it, then review what went wrong (root cause analysis + 5 why's) and then ask the AI to add a tests and gates so that whole class of problem could never reach live again. So I get two levels of regression tests.

One example. Early code used a database date function that worked fine on SQLite in development and silently did the wrong thing on the live Postgres database. It hit me more than once. Now a check scans every change for that exact pattern and fails the build if it finds it. I haven't seen that bug come up for over a month now - and sometimes when I stop to watch the AI talking to itself it catches the issues and fixes it before I even jump in to manually QA things.

Multiply that by every mistake I've made in three months - and it's a lot then the harness, regression tests get so much stronger that it gets harder to ship buggy and broken code.

A few of the gates that earn their keep:

* **A planning gate** that runs before any code. It reads the relevant code, asks me up to five pointed questions, and prints a short working agreement. Nothing gets built until the plan is explicit. I took inspiration from the "grill me" skill and adapted it.
* **An impact gate** before any change to a game rule or balance number. It surfaces everything the change touches, the code, the docs that promised players a number, the tests pinning the old value, and makes me confirm the trade-off out loud. I have a full /doc/ directory of game mechanics, the wiki, and internal economy numbers anchored on a single resource.
* **A reconcile gate** that audits the live game against the handbook/wiki, the source of truth, and shows me where code and docs have drifted apart in either direction.

Then a release pipeline: commit stages only this session's files and runs a quality gate, release won't run without a same-day review passing green, and CI type-checks everything and runs the test suites across six parallel shards before a merge can deploy.

A change that used to reach live in seconds now takes up to ten minutes. That felt slow until I noticed the thing that actually hurt was never speed-to-live, it was how often I had to drop everything and hotfix a live game. That number is close to zero now.

If you're interested in more drop a message on here or [check out my devlog](https://inselnova.com/chronicle/devlog/). I love sharing the journey.

comments.body: This does not appear to be promoting a commercial game (or product). I'm swapping the flair to discussion.

comments.author: TanMojo
comments.body:
One needs a harness and an acute awareness of how their code works. Gating and testing are definitely the right philosophy here. I'm building a text-based narrative walking simulator for AI agents only. The amount of work needed to ensure that the narrative output is consistent and compelling takes many layers of instruction: descriptor files of every terrain type with built in gates, prohibitions, required/allowed/disallowed elements, various environmental profiles, strict rules on improvisation, what can't be invented or hallucinated, and instructions for light/moisture/sound/vegetation/visibility/movement/seasonal/time of day/weather/player agent condition.

Making a game is easy with AI. Making it work without bugs and with consistent performance is the hard part.

comments.author: Useful_Use_6170
comments.body: Nice! Really like the UI! And a bit of the animation honestly that is where most struggle, how did you workflow thru that if you don’t mind sharing your process ?

replies.author: DarrenMoore
replies.body:
Thanks for the comment!

I take a personal passion on trying to make things look nice. I've always worked with designers so I know the principles but this game is as good as I can manage.

I started a lot with gemini. First just told Gemini what type of game I was making, copying and pasting game docs etc.. setting the period then asking it to generate some example screens for me. I'd do this over various gemini chat sessions and then find something I liked. Then I'd ask it to extract just that one element out. I'd save the element (e.g. a house), then bring it into another session and ask the AI to fully explain the image, the colours, shading etc.. until i got a prompt that somewhat explained it.

When I wanted, say a farm i'd copy that image into the prompt (as an attachment), copy the prompt in, and then add in about the farm.

I did it quite a few times and then started to make things like banners etc.. so I was able to build up an [art-and-direction.md](http://art-and-direction.md) file that explains the entire style. Each time it renders something slightly wrong I'd amend it.

Now I can just drop that file into gemini or chatgpt and explain the image I want and I'll get something that "feels" like my game. Though it's still obviously AI.

But then I automated it, I use the prompt, asked an AI agent to make a tool that calls the API's, inject prompts for like, banners, buildings, research, goods, etc.. and then it gives me back the image in less than a minute. It's made generating assets really quick. I can basically add 10 good items to the game and have a decent set of images for each of them in a minute.

For the island and animation. That's all generated with javascript and canvas. That was just slowly and carefully done with prompts and making sure there was a decent "rendering" set of scripts. For the first release it was actually static, but it felt stale so I just worked with the AI to add animations in and then used Chrome dev tools to monitor FPS and then optimise it by shouting at the AI.

The main interface is just CSS. Again, by my instructions to the AI.

replies.body: Wow! I never would of thought of that! So you pretty much asked AI what’s the “code” version of this image or for example “json” format file of this image

replies.author: DarrenMoore
replies.body:
I just asked it to explain the image in normal language. AI is mostly trained on natural language so lean into what it does best.

For the tool. It just sends the same prompt. Nothing pushing the AI towards code.
